what_happened: Experiment E (parallel scaling) measured `time(() => pool.process(items))`. `time()` is synchronous and `pool.process()` returns a Promise, so it recorded only promise-creation time (~800 microseconds), not the awaited work. The first smoke run reported speedup 32x and efficiency 3212% — physically impossible on a 4-core host.
root_cause: Applying a synchronous timer to an asynchronous operation. The awaited work happened outside the measured window.
what_i_did_wrong: Wrote a timing wrapper for an async call without awaiting inside the wrapper. The absurd 32x/3212% numbers were the tell; the correct reaction is to distrust any super-linear speedup, not to report it.
detection: Speedup 32x and efficiency 3212% in the --quick smoke run, far above the 4-core ceiling.
fix: Measure with performance.now() around `await pool.process(items)`. Also added a warmup batch before the measured phase, because the first worker job is JIT-cold and inflated per-worker cost. After the fix, peak speedup is 1.10x at W=4 — consistent with the physical core count.
lesson: Never wrap an async operation in a synchronous timer. Treat any speedup above the core count as a measurement bug until proven otherwise.
